Under the central dogma of molecular biology, genetic information usually flows two ways:

{{c1::DNA → DNA::direction of flow}} — during its transmission from generation to generation

{{c1::DNA → protein::direction of flow}} — during its phenotypic expression in an organism

Why: DNA → DNA is replication, carried out by a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase; DNA → protein is gene expression, run as transcription and then translation.

Roster: DNA → DNA (replication) · DNA → protein (transcription, then translation) · RNA → RNA (replication of RNA viruses) · RNA → DNA (RNA tumor virus genome → DNA proviral form)

Text: Genetic information moves from DNA to protein in two steps: (1) {{c1::transcription::process}}, the transfer of information from {{c2::DNA to RNA::direction of flow}}, and (2) {{c1::translation::process}}, the transfer of information from {{c2::RNA to protein::direction of flow}}.

Text: Messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are the RNA molecules that are {{c1::translated on ribosomes::their fate}}.

Distinguish: mRNA is the only one of the five RNA classes that is translated — tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA are final products in their own right.

Text: In {{c1::eukaryotes::prokaryotes or eukaryotes}}, the primary transcript usually is a {{c2::precursor to the mRNA::relation to the mRNA}} and so is called a {{c2::pre-mRNA::name}}.

Text:
E. coli has two types of transcription terminator, classified by whether termination needs a protein called {{c1::rho (ρ)}}:

{{c1::rho-dependent}} terminators end transcription only in the presence of that protein

{{c1::rho-independent}} terminators end transcription without that protein
Back Extra:
Distinguish: both terminator types make RNA polymerase pause at an RNA hairpin; a rho-dependent terminator adds a 50–90 base-pair C-rich, G-poor stretch upstream of the inverted repeats (a stretch whose RNA forms no hairpin) and a rut (rho utilization) site near the 3′ end of the transcript.

Mechanism: rho binds the rut sequence of the transcript, travels 5′ to 3′ behind RNA polymerase, catches up while the polymerase is paused at the hairpin, and unwinds the DNA/RNA pairing with its helicase activity to release the transcript.

Meaning: termination begins when RNA polymerase encounters a termination signal; the transcription complex then dissociates and releases the nascent RNA.

Introns are removed by three splicing mechanisms, each tied to its own class of precursor RNA (substrate → machinery):

{{c2::tRNA::which precursor RNA}} precursors → {{c1::a splicing endonuclease and a splicing ligase::machinery}}

some {{c2::rRNA::which precursor RNA}} precursors → {{c1::the RNA itself, autocatalytically (no protein enzyme)::machinery}}

nuclear {{c2::pre-mRNA (hnRNA)::which precursor RNA}} transcripts → {{c1::a spliceosome::machinery}}

Text: In type 2 splicing (self-splicing) the intron is excised by {{c1::two::how many}} phosphoester bond transfers, after which the excised intron can {{c2::circularize::what it does}} by one more transfer. Because every step is a bond transfer with {{c3::no bonds lost or gained::net bond change}}, the reaction needs {{c3::no::no / an}} external energy source.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: transfer 1 — the phosphoester bond at the exon 1–intron junction moves onto the guanosine's 3′-OH, cutting exon 1 free; transfer 2 — the bond at the intron–exon 2 junction moves onto the 3′ end of exon 1, joining the two exons; a third, internal transfer then closes the excised intron into a circle.

Distinguish: spliceosomal (type 3) splicing is also two steps, but its first step requires ATP hydrolysis and no guanosine.

Why: the circularization of the excised intron on its own shows that the self-splicing activity resides primarily, if not entirely, within the intron itself.
